project_tracker_diagnostic: Deciduous red oak with 7–9 deeply cut lobes ending in sharp bristle/awn tips; glossy mostly glabrous leaves; biennial acorns.
verified_target_counties: Hays; Travis; Blanco; Burnet; Comal; Gillespie; Kerr; Bandera; Edwards; Real; Uvalde; Williamson; Kendall

morphology_keys.bark: Gray and smooth to black and furrowed.
morphology_keys.leaves: Broadly elliptic to obovate/circular; usually 7–9 lobes; lobe tips acute to acuminate with numerous awns/bristles; surfaces mostly glabrous and often glossy.
morphology_keys.acorn: Biennial; cup usually goblet- to cup-shaped and covers roughly one-third to one-half of the nut.
best_field_traits: FNA adult leaf blade usually 55–100 mm long; glabrous to small tufts beneath at vein axils
terminal buds gray-brown/reddish-brown, scales ciliate toward apex
mature cup commonly 5–11.5 mm deep and 10–18 mm wide; shape/depth best read on attached ripe acorns
morphology_keys.joey_field_note: Joey's landscaping video gives a direct crown-and-lobed-leaf field view of Texas red oak. A second Edwards Plateau frame shows a rock-wall/chasmophyte oak that Joey calls 'probably Quercus buckleyi'; retain that second frame only as tentative habitat context, not as a definitive species diagnostic.

photo_strategy.oak_specific_tightening: Prioritize multi-photo late-summer/fall observations to increase the chance of mature leaves and acorns, plus curated taxon reference photos.

look_here_first: Start with several mature, NOT juvenile, bristle-tipped leaves. Then check terminal buds (small, scales distinctly ciliate toward tips) and the mature acorn: a relatively deep goblet/cup-shaped cup commonly enclosing 1/3–1/2 of the nut. Compare against Shumard oak's generally larger, shallower-cupped fruits.

best_tie_breakers: Mature acorn cup: 5–11.5 mm high and 10–18 mm broad, often 1/3–1/2 nut (Buckley) vs. Shumard cup 7–12 mm high, 15–30 mm broad, often 1/4–1/3 nut. Individual values overlap; use relative cup enclosure.
Terminal bud: 2.5–7 mm with distinctly ciliate outer scale margins near tips (Buckley); Shumard more often 4–8 mm, gray-brown, often five-angled and glabrous.
Buckley generally has smaller mature leaves (~55–100 mm long) on dry limestone uplands; Shumard often has larger leaves (~100–200 mm) on more mesic slopes/streambanks.
unreliable_alone: Presence or absence of lower leaf-vein-axil hairs (Buckley may also have small tufts).
Exactly 5 vs 7 vs 9 lobes: ranges overlap and environment affects leaves.
Bark or tree size without other evidence.
diagnostic_comparison.hybrid_guardrail: Q. buckleyi × Q. shumardii intermediates occur; leave unresolved when diagnostic evidence is mixed.
